Well, I've been farming this land for 40 years now, and at 61 I'm not as strong as I used to be. It's just me and my wife in the household, so labor is tight — I have to hire help during the rush times. We have 10 mu of flat land here in Quzhou, and I've always done wheat-maize double cropping. That's not changing.

For the wheat, I plant in early October, right after National Day. I use that improved Jinmai variety — costs me about 28 yuan per mu for seed, but I know it works here. The extension station recommends 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, but after 40 years I know my soil needs a bit more. I apply 17 kg total — 10 kg as base fertilizer before planting, along with phosphate and potash, and then at green-up in March I topdress another 7 kg. Last year I tried less because fertilizer prices were high, and the wheat looked yellow at jointing. Never again. My neighbor Lao Wang did the same and his yield suffered. I also put down some herbicide in spring; we can't weed by hand anymore at our age.

For irrigation, I have the tube well, but pumping costs electricity. I'll water the wheat four times: wintering water in November, then at jointing, heading, and grain filling if the weather stays dry. Better to spend the money on water than risk a drought like we had a few years back.

The maize goes in right after wheat harvest in early June — I have maybe five days, sometimes less. I hire a combine for the wheat, then plant the hybrid maize seed immediately. The hybrid seed costs about 48 yuan per mu, but you can't save your own seed — it doesn't work. For fertilizer, I put down 16 kg of nitrogen for the maize, split between planting and the big trumpet stage. Two irrigations for maize — one at the big trumpet stage and one at silking — that's usually enough unless it's a very dry summer.

I expect about 460 kg per mu for wheat and 500 kg per mu for maize if the weather cooperates. Total input costs will run around 2,700 yuan for the year. It's tight with just two of us, but we've managed before.
